title: The case for writing by hand
text: Keyboards {{1}} taken over the classroom and the meeting room, {{2}} the humble pen refuses to disappear. {{3}} we write by hand, we cannot keep up {{4}} a fast speaker, and {{5}} looks like a defect turns out to be a feature: because every word cannot be captured, the brain must summarise, compress and connect instead. Studies suggest {{6}} students who take notes by longhand remember {{7}} of a lecture a week later than laptop note-takers, who often transcribe without processing. {{8}} is not the slowness itself that helps but the selection it forces — which is why writing anything out by hand, from a revision card to a shopping list, still sticks in the mind so reliably.

gaps.explanation: Present perfect with a plural subject: have taken.

gaps.hint: conjunction: the meeting room, ___ the pen refuses
gaps.explanation: Contrast between conquest and survival: but.

gaps.hint: conjunction: ___ we write by hand, we cannot
gaps.explanation: Time clause governing the claim: when.

gaps.hint: preposition: cannot keep up ___ a fast speaker
gaps.explanation: 'Keep up with' — the fixed phrasal verb.

gaps.hint: pronoun: and ___ looks like a defect
gaps.explanation: Fused relative subject: what looks like a defect.

gaps.hint: pronoun: remember ___ of a lecture a week later
gaps.explanation: The comparative 'more of a lecture' — first element gapped.

gaps.hint: cleft pronoun: ___ is not the slowness itself
gaps.explanation: The cleft structure 'It is not X but Y'.
